tone_statements.quote: One of the most intriguing features of Htanaw phonology is the presence of three lexical tones (four according to some authors). [...] The origin of tones in Htanaw is not known (Gehrmann 2022:104), and a replication of the ‘concept of having lexical tones’ from Burmese is a possibility [...] Tones in Htanaw do not only have lexical function, but they also express grammatical functions. Most prominently, in possessive and oblique contexts, low and mid tones change to high.

tone_statements.citation: Jenny, Mathias, Han Tin, Rachel Weymuth & Alexandra Herdeg. 2024. Sandhi or not? Tone assimilation in Htanaw. Paper presented at ICAAL 12 (International Conference on Austroasiatic Linguistics), Chiang Mai, 2024; abstract (1 p.) online at icaal.net.
tone_statements.quote: Htanaw, spoken in southern Shan State of Myanmar by around 3000 people, has three phonemic tones, namely low-falling, mid-falling, and high-rising. Tones are mainly used for lexical distinction, but they can also express grammatical functions such as possessive and oblique in kinship terms. Nothing is known about the origin of tones in Htanaw, and their phonetic features are subject of an ongoing study. [...] The triggering word must carry high tone, the affected word low or mid tone, which changes to high.

sources.note: Full text: sec. 2.3 'Loan phonology' (p. 98) states Htanaw has three lexical tones (four according to some authors: low-falling, mid-falling, high-rising, table 2), no tone correspondences in Burmese loans, origin of tones unknown (possibly concept replicated from Burmese; proto-Palaungic unlikely tonal, tones maybe recent), complex tone assimilation, and grammatical tone: low/mid -> high marks possessive/oblique on some human nouns/kin terms, parallel to Burmese induced creaky tone.

sources.note: Htanaw has three phonemic tones (low-falling, mid-falling, high-rising), mainly lexical but also grammatical (possessive/oblique in kinship terms); origin of tones unknown; the 'tone sandhi' of Si 2014 is re-analysed as non-automatic tone assimilation (high-tone trigger raises a following low/mid word to high, only its first syllable; conditioned lexically and morphosyntactically: S-V, V-O, V-ADV, N-MDF, NUM-CLF, not inside the verb phrase; may cross clause boundaries; glottal-coda words more prone).
